ety.text: From Middle English game, gamen, gammen, from Old English gamen (“sport, joy, mirth, pastime, game, amusement, pleasure”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną (“amusement, pleasure, game", literally "participation, communion, people together”), from *ga- (collective prefix) + *mann- (“man”); or alternatively from *ga- + a root from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think, have in mind”).

senses.d: A playful activity that may be unstructured; an amusement or pastime.
ex: Being a child is all fun and games.

senses.d: An activity described by a set of rules, especially for the purpose of entertainment, often competitive or having an explicit goal.
ex: Games in the classroom can make learning fun.

senses.d: A school subject during which sports are practised.
ex: From time to time tracksuited boys ran past them, with all the deadly purpose and humourless concentration of those who enjoyed Games.

senses.d: A particular instance of playing a game.
ex: Sally won the game.
They can turn the game around in the second half.

senses.d: Part of a set during which one player continuously serves (at least four rallies must be won to win a game, at least six games must be won to win the set).
ex: Game, set and match!

senses.d: That which is gained, such as the stake in a game.
The number of points necessary to win a game.
ex: In short whist, five points are game, while in in table tennis game is 21 points.
See also: for the win

senses.d: In some games, a point awarded to the player whose cards add up to the largest sum.
The equipment that enables such activity, particularly as packaged under a title.
ex: Some of the games in the closet we have on the computer as well.

senses.d: One's manner, style, or performance in playing a game.
ex: Study can help your game of chess.
Hit the gym if you want to toughen up your game.

senses.d: Willing and able to participate.
ex: "[…] But what’s this long face about, Mr. Starbuck; wilt thou not chase the white whale? art not game for Moby Dick?”

senses.d: That shows a tendency to continue to fight against another animal, despite being wounded, often severely.
Persistent, especially in senses similar to the above.
To gamble.
To play card games, board games, or video games.
To exploit loopholes in a system or bureaucracy in a way which defeats or nullifies the spirit of the rules in effect, usually to obtain a result which otherwise would be unobtainable.
ex: We'll bury them in paperwork, and game the system.

senses.d: To perform premeditated seduction strategy.
ex: Returning briefly to his journalistic persona to interview Britney Spears, he finds himself gaming her, and she gives him her phone number.
A business associate of mine at the time, George Wu, sat across the way, gaming a stripper the way I taught him.

senses.d: Injured, lame.
